newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba, U.S. begin talks on migration accords.
newsitem.headline: Cuba, U.S. begin talks on migration accords.

text.p: Cuba and the United States began talks to review immigration accords in Havana on Wednesday in the first official public contact between the two countries since President Bill Clinton was re-elected last month.

The meeting was expected to last until Thursday. The sides were led by Cuban parliamentary president Ricardo Alarcon, a former foreign minister who headed Cuba's delegation at earlier migration talks, and John Hamilton, U.S. deputy assistant secretary of state for Central American and Caribbean affairs.
Neither delegation spoke as they entered the Convention Centre. No official comment was expected until Thursday.

Washington and Havana do not have diplomatic ties but they have held periodic meetings to discuss immigration accords they signed in September 1994 and May 1995 aimed at halting illegal Cuban immigrantion to the United States. They last met for such talks in November 1995 in New York.

Since then there has been a notable chill in already frosty U.S.-Cuba relations, triggered by Cuba's shooting down of two small private American planes flown by Cuban exiles in February and Washington's subsequent tightening of its longstanding economic embargo on the Communist-ruled island.
Cuban officials say these tensions delayed the latest round of talks.

Both Cuba and the United States have said they are generally satisfied with implementation of the accords, reached after the "rafter crisis" of August and September 1994 in which more than 30,000 Cubans left the island on rafts and other flimsy vessels for Florida.

The accords stemmed the flow of Cuban boat people and the maximum of 30 to 40 people intercepted by U.S. authorities each month has been well below past years. But both sides have said they have some areas of concern.

Cuba has said it wants Washington to return four Cubans accused of hijacking small planes from Cuba in two incidents in July and August. Washington has said it will put them on trial in the United States and does not intend to return them.

Despite its reservations, Cuba cooperated with the United States in prosecuting one of the alleged hijackers, former Interior Ministry official Jose Fernandez Pupo, who faces trial in the United States next April.

Cuba also is concerned that not all illegal migrants intercepted by U.S. authorities are returned home. More than 480 illegal Cuban migrants have been sent home by U.S. authorities since May 1995 but about 50 who were intercepted have not been returned.

The United States says in some cases this has been because the Cubans were transferred to the United States for medical reasons and then asked for asylum. In other cases, U.S. authorities thought they might face persecution in Cuba.

Meanwhile, Washington says it is meeting its requirement to grant 20,000 visas annually to Cubans, but not all those people are able to travel, sometimes because of the high cost and sometimes because they are not granted exit permits.

Fees to emigrate are about $400 for a medical test, $150 for an exit visa and $50 for a passport, as well as more than $300 for a plane ticket, which is a small fortune for Cubans. Washington says the fees should be reduced.
